tips.title: Track Every Dollar for One Week
tips.summary: Spend a single week writing down every purchase, no matter how small. Awareness is the first step to control.
tips.body: Before you can improve your finances, you have to know where the money goes. Use a notes app or a small notebook and log every coffee, snack, or subscription charge. At the end of the week, categorize the spending. You'll often be surprised by how much leaks out on small, frequent purchases. This simple habit builds the foundation for every budget you'll ever create.

tips.title: Follow the 50/30/20 Rule
tips.summary: Allocate 50% of income to needs, 30% to wants, and 20% to savings or debt repayment.
tips.body: The 50/30/20 rule is one of the simplest budgeting frameworks for students. Half of your income covers essentials like rent, groceries, and transit. Thirty percent goes to lifestyle choices like dining out and entertainment. The final twenty percent is non-negotiable — it pays future you through savings or by chipping away at student loans. Adjust the ratios as needed, but always protect that 20%.

tips.title: Use the 24-Hour Purchase Rule
tips.summary: Wait 24 hours before buying anything over $25 to cut impulse spending.
tips.body: Impulse purchases are budget killers. When you see something you want, add it to a wishlist and walk away for a full day. If you still want it tomorrow and you can afford it, go ahead. More often than not, the urge fades. This tiny pause protects your wallet from dozens of small decisions you'll regret later.

tips.title: Build a $500 Starter Emergency Fund
tips.summary: Before investing or aggressive debt payoff, save a $500 cushion for small emergencies.
tips.body: A small emergency fund prevents life's curveballs from turning into debt. A flat tire, a surprise co-pay, or a broken laptop charger shouldn't blow up your budget. Aim for $500 first — it's reachable in a few months and it covers roughly 90% of common student emergencies. Once you have it, you can grow it toward three months of expenses.

tips.title: Automate Your Savings
tips.summary: Set up an automatic transfer on payday so you save before you can spend.
tips.body: Relying on willpower to save is a losing game. Schedule a recurring transfer from your checking account to a savings account the day after you get paid. Treat it like a non-negotiable bill. Even $25 per paycheck compounds into hundreds over a year — and you barely feel the difference day to day.

tips.title: Open a High-Yield Savings Account
tips.summary: Move idle cash into a high-yield savings account to earn 10–20x more interest.
tips.body: Most big bank savings accounts pay almost nothing. Online high-yield savings accounts typically offer 4% or more in today's environment, with the same FDIC insurance. The switch takes about ten minutes, and the money earns money while you sleep. Perfect for emergency funds and short-term goals.

tips.title: Start Investing With Just $5
tips.summary: Use fractional shares and low-fee brokers to begin investing with pocket change.
tips.body: You don't need thousands to start investing. Many modern brokerages allow you to buy fractional shares of index funds for as little as $5. The earlier you start, the more time compound growth has to work in your favor. A 22-year-old who invests $50/month can have over $100,000 by age 62, even with conservative returns.

tips.title: Understand the Power of Compound Interest
tips.summary: Interest earns interest — time in the market beats timing the market.
tips.body: Compound interest is interest earned on your interest. A single $1,000 investment at 8% annual return grows to over $10,000 in 30 years without adding a single dollar. Time is the most powerful variable in investing. Start embarrassingly small if you must — just start.

tips.title: Prefer Low-Cost Index Funds
tips.summary: Index funds outperform most actively managed funds over the long run — and cost less.
tips.body: Index funds track the whole market instead of trying to beat it. Their expense ratios are often under 0.10%, compared to 1%+ for actively managed funds. Lower fees mean more of your money stays invested and compounds. For most students, a simple three-fund portfolio is more than enough.

tips.title: Avoid Lifestyle Inflation
tips.summary: When income rises, hold the line on spending and bank the difference.
tips.body: A raise, a stipend increase, or a new job can quietly destroy your finances if every dollar gets spent. Commit to keeping your lifestyle stable for at least 6 months after any income jump. Direct the extra money to savings, debt, or investments. This single habit separates people who build wealth from people who just earn more.

tips.title: Know the Difference Between Good and Bad Debt
tips.summary: Not all debt is equal — student loans for a degree are not the same as credit card debt.
tips.body: Debt that funds an appreciating asset (education, a small business) can be considered good debt. Debt for depreciating items or consumption (credit card balances, luxury goods) almost always costs more than it's worth. Before taking on debt, ask: will this purchase be worth more to me in five years than the interest I'll pay?

tips.title: Build Credit Early and Carefully
tips.summary: A student credit card used responsibly is one of the fastest ways to build credit history.
tips.body: Landlords, car loans, and even some employers look at your credit score. Get a student credit card, use it for one small recurring bill (like a streaming service), and pay it off in full every month. After a year of on-time payments, your score will thank you. Never charge more than you can pay off that same month.

tips.title: Cook at Home More Often
tips.summary: Cutting dining out to once a week can save the average student over $1,500 per year.
tips.body: Restaurant and delivery costs add up fast. A $15 lunch five days a week is $3,900 a year. A homemade lunch using $4 of ingredients is just $1,040 — saving nearly $2,900. You don't have to give up eating out entirely, but being intentional about it is one of the fastest ways to free up cash for goals that actually matter.

tips.title: Use Student Discounts Everywhere
tips.summary: Your student ID can save you 10–50% on software, transit, food, and entertainment.
tips.body: Many companies offer student pricing that's barely advertised. From Spotify and Apple Music to Adobe Creative Cloud, Microsoft 365, and even Amazon Prime Student, the savings stack up fast. Always check before you buy — and don't forget local businesses near campus that offer student rates on gym memberships, food, and services.

tips.title: Review Subscriptions Quarterly
tips.summary: Cancel or downgrade at least one subscription every three months.
tips.body: Subscriptions are silent budget leaks. Pick a date every three months to audit what you're paying for. Cancel anything you haven't used in the last 30 days. Most services offer annual plans at a discount if you genuinely need them — but only commit to annual pricing if you already know you use them regularly.

tips.title: Set Specific Financial Goals
tips.summary: Vague goals fail. Replace 'I should save more' with 'I will save $1,200 by May.'
tips.body: Goals that lack a number and a deadline are wishes. Use the SMART framework: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. 'Save $1,200 for a summer internship travel fund by May 15' tells you exactly what to do every month. Track progress visibly — a thermometer chart on your wall works wonders.

tips.title: Negotiate Your Bills
tips.summary: Call your phone, internet, and insurance providers once a year to ask for lower rates.
tips.body: Most service providers would rather give you a discount than lose you as a customer. A 15-minute phone call once a year can knock 10–25% off your cell phone, internet, and insurance bills. Be polite, mention competitor offers, and ask what they can do. The worst they can say is no — but they rarely do.

tips.title: Build a Sinking Fund for Big Purchases
tips.summary: Save monthly for known future expenses (laptop, textbooks, travel) instead of using credit.
tips.body: A sinking fund is a small savings pool earmarked for a future expense. Divide the cost by the months until you need it, and set that amount aside automatically. When the purchase date arrives, you pay cash — no debt, no stress. This works for laptops, textbooks, conference fees, and even holiday gifts.
